docs.title: Weir
docs.text:
Scripts that glue programs together, checked before they run.

Get started GitHub

Weir is a small interpreted language for anything you would otherwise write in bash and run from a terminal, a cron job, a systemd unit or a pipeline. A script has a shape: inputs, a sequence of steps, some outputs. Shell languages leave that shape implied. Weir makes it the language, and checks it before anything runs.

sandbox {
  mount system
  mount "/var/log" ro                 // the only part of the machine this script can see
}

main flow report {
  in  log: path = path(text: "/var/log/dpkg.log")
  in  since: duration = 7d
  in  top: int = 10
  out changes: int

  let events = load(log: log).events
    .filter(where: it.epoch >= now_epoch() - since.seconds)

  summary {
    for p in events.count_by(key: it.package).sort_by(key: it.count, order: desc).take(n: top) {
      print(text: "${p.key}\t${p.count}")
    }
  }
  set changes = events.count()
}

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Typed inputs become the command line. --help is generated, and a bad value is rejected before the first step runs (weir exits with return code 2).
  • Commands take argument lists, not strings. There is no shell, so quoting bugs cannot be written.
  • Every script declares the filesystem it runs in. The sandbox block is enforced with Linux namespaces, including for every program the script starts. Nothing prompts.
  • weir check finds problems first. Each one has a stable code, a position and a fix hint, in terms of what you wrote.
  • Steps that change things are confirmable. They are skipped, and reported as skipped, unless the caller passes --confirm.
  • Tests are part of the file. weir test runs them with program output stubbed.

docs.title: Why Weir
docs.text: A weir is a low barrier across a river. It doesn't stop the water; it controls how the water passes — over a defined edge, through a known channel, at a measurable rate. Engineers build them precisely because a weir makes flow visible and countable. That is what this language does with scripts. Work is expressed as flows, data moves through pipelines, and nothing passes unseen: a script declares its inputs, its steps, its outputs and the resources it may touch, and the checker verifies all of it before a single command runs.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Early, and subject to change

The interpreter runs the examples in this repository and the worked examples in the design document. The language, its syntax and its tooling are subject to change. Implementation status lists what is built, what is not, and the decisions made where the design was silent.

docs.title: Weir: Design Document
docs.text: Status: early design, with a reference interpreter. The language, its syntax and its tooling are all subject to change, and several sections end in open questions. This document is the specification. IMPLEMENTATION.md records what the interpreter in src/ implements, what it does not, and the decisions made where this document was silent.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Scripts that glue programs together are still mostly written in bash. Bash is everywhere, but both people and AI models make the same predictable mistakes in it: unquoted expansions, word splitting, rm -rf "$DIR/" with an empty $DIR, forgotten set -e, pipelines that hide failures, secrets on the command line, and scripts that prompt and hang under cron. Almost all of these are detectable by static analysis, but bash's grammar makes that analysis unreliable, and the mistakes are legal programs.

CI workflow files (GitHub Actions and similar) have a better structure: typed inputs, named steps, declared outputs. They then wrap that structure around YAML and shell strings, which loses the safety the structure could have provided.

Weir is an interpreted language for scripts that takes the structural shape of a workflow file and makes it the language itself. It targets anything otherwise written in bash and run from a terminal, a cron job, a systemd unit or a CI pipeline. CI is one use case, not the model. Its design goal is that the mistakes above cannot be expressed, or are rejected by weir check before anything runs, with an error message precise enough for a person or a model to fix without guessing.

Non-goals: Weir is not a general-purpose language, not an interactive shell, and not a build system. It does not try to be fast at computation.
