docs.title: Using Weir in CI
docs.text: A Weir script is a command line program, so a CI job runs it as one step. The CI system decides when a job runs. The script decides what the job does.

docs.title: A workflow
docs.text:
name: nginx-check
on: [push]

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install Weir
        run: cargo install --git https://github.com/johnjoeallen/weir --tag v0.3.0

      - name: Check and test
        run: |
          weir check ci/deploy.weir
          weir test ci/deploy.weir

      - name: Run
        env:
          WEIR_SECRET_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
        run: weir run ci/deploy.weir --json

weir check and weir test need no sandbox and read no secrets, so they work on any runner. weir test stubs every program, so it runs nothing real.

docs.title: What a step can rely on
docs.text:
• Return codes. 0 is success and 1 is a failed flow. 2 is a usage error and 3 means weir check found errors. 4 means a capability was denied, including a sandbox that could not be created. A step fails on any non-zero code, and the number says why.
  • Secrets. A secret input is read from WEIR_SECRET_<NAME>, --secret-file or --secret-stdin, never from an option, so it doesn't appear in the process list.
  • No terminal. Steps marked confirmable are skipped unless --confirm is given, and --plan prints what would happen without running it.
  • Machine-readable results. --json prints one document with the outputs, the steps and "sandbox": true or false. weir check --json does the same for errors.

docs.title: When the runner can't build the sandbox
docs.text:
The sandbox needs unprivileged user namespaces. Some runners forbid them: a hardened kernel, an AppArmor setting, or a container job whose seccomp profile blocks unshare and pivot_root. With the default mode, required, the step then fails with return code 4 and the message names the cause.

If the job is already isolated, as in a container, set the mode once for the job instead of changing the script:

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container: debian:stable
    env:
      WEIR_SANDBOX: auto
  • auto builds the sandbox when it can. When it can't, the log shows a warning with the cause and the script runs without it. The result records "sandbox": false.
  • off never builds it. Use it when you know the runner can't, so the log doesn't carry a probe failure on every run.
  • A script can't set its own mode, so a pull request that edits the script can't turn the sandbox off. The mode is part of the workflow file, which reviewers can see.

Without a sandbox the script's mount lines don't restrict anything, and paths aren't remapped. A script with a mount that remaps a path (mount logs at "/logs" ro) can't run that way. See When the sandbox cannot be created.

Not yet verified on hosted runners

Whether GitHub-hosted runners allow unprivileged user namespaces depends on the runner image and its kernel settings, and has not been checked here. Run weir run once with the default mode to see. If it exits with return code 4, use auto.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
weir run   <file> [flow] [options]     run a flow (the `main` flow by default)
weir check <file> [--json]             check a script without running anything
weir list  <file> [--manifest]         list flows, their inputs and outputs
weir test  [path]                      run the `test` blocks of a file or folder
weir lock  [file]                      pin remote components (none are supported yet)
weir sandbox suggest <file>            not implemented yet
weir --version | --help

docs.title: Running a script directly
docs.text:
weir FILE with a script as the first argument is the form a shebang line uses. A script that starts with

#!/usr/bin/env -S weir --run

runs when executed: ./script.weir [flow] [options]. The kernel turns that into weir --run ./script.weir .... The -S is needed because Linux passes everything after the interpreter path as a single argument, and plain env would look for a program literally named weir --run.

--run is required on purpose. With a plain #!/usr/bin/env weir line, executing the script only shows its help and exits with return code 2, so a file never acts by accident. You can also pass it yourself: weir script.weir --run. weir run script.weir always runs.

The other modes are subcommands only: weir check FILE, weir test FILE and weir list FILE.

Typing weir check with no path means the check command. A file that happens to have a command's name needs a path, as in weir run ./check. Executing it directly is unaffected, because the kernel passes its full path.

docs.title: Options generated from inputs
docs.text:
Each input a flow declares becomes a command-line option of the same name.

  • in top: int = 10 becomes --top <int>. The default, 10, is shown in --help.
  • A list<T> input is given by repeating its option: --tag a --tag b.
  • A bool input becomes a pair of switches, --name and --no-name.
  • A value that cannot be read as the input's type is a usage error. weir exits with return code 2, and the message names the option.
  • A path value is a path on the host. Weir translates it to the path inside the sandbox through the sandbox mounts.

docs.title: Run options
docs.text:
Option Effect --confirm also run confirmable steps --plan print what would happen and run nothing (a dry run) --json print one JSON result document; print goes to stderr --out <name> print one named output as raw text; print goes to stderr --ro <inside-path> turn a rw mount into ro for this run --deny-exec <name> refuse to start a program for this run --secret-file <name>=<path> read a secret input from a file (mode 0600) --secret-stdin <name> read a secret input from stdin --sandbox <mode> required (the default), auto or off; see the sandbox. WEIR_SANDBOX sets it too --no-sandbox the same as --sandbox off --help show the options a script generates from its inputs

A secret input is never accepted on the command line. It comes from WEIR_SECRET_<NAME>, --secret-file or --secret-stdin.

docs.text: Code Meaning 0 success 1 a flow failed 2 usage error 3 weir check found errors 4 capability denied, including a sandbox that cannot be created

docs.title: Running programs
docs.text:
Weir starts a program as an argument list. There is no shell, so nothing is split on spaces, expanded or re-parsed, and the quoting bugs that bash scripts have cannot be written. Every snippet on this page comes from examples/commands.weir, which you can run with weir run examples/commands.weir.

There are two ways to start a program: a declared filter, and the generic run.

docs.title: A declared filter
docs.text:
A filter wraps exactly one program. It names the program, its typed parameters, how the program reads input and what it produces, and the part of the disk it can see.

filter cat_file {
  program "cat"
  in file: path
  args ["--", file]          // a list; "--" stops a file named "-x" being read as an option
  see system
  see "/etc" ro            // this program can see /etc and nothing else the script mounted
  takes none                 // stdin is closed
  yields lines               // stdout becomes a list of lines
}

Call it like a function, with named arguments:

let passwd = cat_file(file: path(text: "/etc/passwd"))

takes and yields are each one of none, lines, text or json. A filter that takes lines reads the lines before it in a chain:

filter grep_fixed {
  program "grep"
  in pattern: string
  args ["-F", "-e", pattern]
  see system
  takes lines
  yields lines
  ok_codes [0, 1]            // grep returns 1 for "no match", which is not a failure here
}

set found = passwd.grep_fixed(pattern: pattern)

The . joins them. The lines from passwd become the standard input of grep.

docs.title: The generic run
docs.text:
For a one-off call that doesn't need a declaration:

let kernel = run(cmd: "uname", args: ["-s", "-r"])

It returns the program's output as a list of lines. cmd must be a literal string, so the program is known before the script runs, and weir check can test it against the sandbox. A computed program name is the error E-DYNAMIC-CMD.

Spread a list into the arguments with ...$name:

let words = ["one", "two", "three"]
let echoed = run(cmd: "echo", args: ["words:", ...$words])

No shell strings

run(cmd: "tar -czf a b") doesn't split the string. It looks for a program with that whole text as its name. Starting a shell (sh, bash) and passing it a string is allowed but weir check warns about it (W-SHELL-STRING), because the string is re-parsed, which is what Weir is designed to avoid.

docs.title: When a program fails
docs.text:
A return code outside ok_codes throws ExecError. The default is [0], so a failure stops the script unless you say otherwise. There is nothing like set -e to forget.

Three ways to deal with it:

List the return codes that are fine.

// grep -c prints a count, and returns 1 when the count is zero.
let no_match = run(cmd: "grep", args: ["-c", "-F", "-e", "no-such-text-zzz", "/etc/hostname"], ok_codes: [0, 1])

try turns a failure into a value. The attempt has ok, code and message, and try itself never throws:

let attempt = try run(cmd: "false", args: [])
print(text: "false ${describe(code: attempt.code)}")

catch handles a typed error:

try {
  cat_file(file: path(text: "/etc/no-such-file"))
} catch e: ExecError {
  print(text: "cat failed as expected: ${e.message}")
}

fail message: "..." stops the script with return code 1 and your message.

docs.title: Restricting several commands: within
docs.text:
A filter's see lines narrow one program. To narrow a stretch of the script, put it in a within block, which can also return a value:

let info = within system, "/etc" ro {
  let kernel = run(cmd: "uname", args: ["-s", "-r"])
  let hosts  = cat_file(file: path(text: "/etc/hosts"))
  return { kernel: first(of: kernel), hosts: count(of: hosts) }
}

Inside the block /var/log doesn't exist for any program or built-in, even though the script mounts it. See The sandbox.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
A test never starts a real program. It gives each filter the lines it would yield:

test "search finds the matching lines" {
  stub cat_file yields lines: ["root:x:0:0", "daemon:x:1:1", "root2:x:2:2"]
  stub grep_fixed yields lines: ["root:x:0:0", "root2:x:2:2"]
  let r = run search(pattern: "root")
  expect count(of: r.found) == 2
}

A filter without a stub fails the test and tells you the line to add. The generic run has no stub, so put the calls you want to test in filters, and keep one-off run calls in flows that the tests don't call.

docs.title: Programs that change things
docs.text:
A step that changes the system goes in a confirmable block. It's skipped, and reported as skipped, unless the caller passes --confirm. See examples/logwatch.weir, which edits a deny file and reloads nginx this way.

The design document has the full rules.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The scripts are in the examples/ folder and are installed under /usr/share/doc/weir/examples/ by the Debian package.

Script What it does commands.weir Every way Weir starts a program: declared filters, chaining, the generic run, ok_codes, try and catch. See Running programs. Read-only. dpkgwatch.weir Summarises package changes from dpkg.log: counts by action, most-changed packages, busiest days, and removed packages. Read-only. logwatch.weir Summarises an nginx access log and can block abusive clients by editing a deny file, with confirmable steps, a lock, and a rollback if nginx -t rejects the change. parse_access.weir A local component imported by logwatch.weir: parses nginx combined-format lines into typed records with pure date arithmetic, so no program is started per line. 
./examples/dpkgwatch.weir --top 5
weir test examples/dpkgwatch.weir
weir run examples/logwatch.weir block --log /var/log/nginx/access.log --plan

The design document contains two longer worked examples, a log analysis with a config change and a certificate expiry checker.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
Rust 1.89 or later. Weir has no dependencies.

git clone https://github.com/johnjoeallen/weir
cd weir
cargo build --release        # target/release/weir
cargo test

docs.title: As a Debian package
docs.text:
cargo install cargo-deb
scripts/build-deb.sh         # builds target/debian/weir_*.deb, then bumps the build number
sudo apt install ./target/debian/weir_*.deb

The binary is installed as /usr/bin/weir. The docs and the example scripts go under /usr/share/doc/weir/. The package links the host libc dynamically.

Platform

The sandbox requires Linux with unprivileged user namespaces enabled. Weir has only been tested on Linux (x86_64). If the sandbox cannot be created, weir run exits with return code 4. --sandbox auto runs the script without a sandbox, with a warning, only if the sandbox cannot be created. --sandbox off never builds one.

docs.title: Run an example
docs.text:
examples/dpkgwatch.weir summarises package activity from /var/log/dpkg.log:

weir run examples/dpkgwatch.weir
weir run examples/dpkgwatch.weir --log /var/log/dpkg.log.2.gz --since 30d --top 20
weir run examples/dpkgwatch.weir --help        # options generated from the script's inputs

docs.title: Make a script executable
docs.text:
A script that starts with #!/usr/bin/env -S weir --run runs when executed:

./examples/dpkgwatch.weir --top 5

With a plain #!/usr/bin/env weir line, executing the file only shows the script's help and exits with return code 2. Nothing runs by accident. See Command line for why -S is needed.

docs.title: Small example
docs.text:
The script as a whole can see /etc and /var/log, both read-only. Each of its two filters gets a smaller view: cat_hosts sees /etc but not /var/log, and count_lines sees /var/log but not /etc. The test stubs both programs, so it runs nothing.

#!/usr/bin/env -S weir --run

// The script as a whole can see /etc and /var/log, both read-only.
sandbox {
  mount system
  mount "/etc" ro
  mount "/var/log" ro
}

// This filter can see /etc but not /var/log.
filter cat_hosts {
  program "cat"
  in file: path
  args ["--", file]
  see system
  see "/etc" ro
  takes none
  yields lines
}

// This filter can see /var/log but not /etc.
filter count_lines {
  program "wc"
  in file: path
  args ["-l", file]
  see system
  see "/var/log" ro
  takes none
  yields lines
}

main flow hosts {
  in  file: path = path(text: "/etc/hosts")
  out n: int

  let rows = cat_hosts(file: file)
    .filter(where: not starts_with(text: it, prefix: "#"))
  for r in rows {
    print(text: r)
  }
  print(text: "dpkg.log: ${first(of: count_lines(file: path(text: "/var/log/dpkg.log")))}")
  set n = rows.count()
}

test "counts the lines that are not comments" {
  stub cat_hosts yields lines: ["# comment", "127.0.0.1 localhost"]
  stub count_lines yields lines: ["42 /var/log/dpkg.log"]
  let r = run hosts()
  expect r.n == 1
}

Save it as hosts.weir and make it executable with chmod +x hosts.weir. Then:

weir check hosts.weir     # static check, nothing runs
weir test  hosts.weir     # run the test block with the programs stubbed
./hosts.weir              # run it (the shebang line supplies --run)

To see the restriction work, point the first filter at a file it can't see:

./hosts.weir --file /var/log/dpkg.log
# error in hosts: ExecError: `cat -- /var/log/dpkg.log` exited with code 1:
#   cat: /var/log/dpkg.log: No such file or directory

The file exists on the host and the script mounts it, but cat_hosts has no /var/log in its view.

The full language is described in the design document.

docs.title: The sandbox
docs.text:
A script declares the part of the machine it can see in a sandbox block at the top of the script you run. Weir builds that view first and then runs the script inside it, together with every program the script starts. A directory the block doesn't mount isn't hidden or read-only. It simply isn't there. Paths written in the script refer to this view, not to the host.

sandbox {
  mount system                      // the usual program directories, read-only
  mount "/var/log/nginx" rw
  mount "/etc/nginx" ro
}

A filter can restrict what its program sees by adding see lines to its declaration. This one runs nginx -t, which needs the config and its own error log:

filter nginx_test {
  program "nginx"
  args ["-t"]
  see system
  see "/etc/nginx" ro
  see "/var/log/nginx" rw       // nginx -t opens its error log
  takes none
  yields none
}

The program sees only the paths listed there, and only those that the script's own sandbox block mounted. A filter with no see lines sees everything the script mounted. A see line can only narrow: see "/etc/nginx" rw would be an error here, because the script mounts it read-only. Only the script you run has a sandbox block. A script it imports with use can't mount anything, so imported code never sees more than the script you run allows.

docs.title: How it is enforced
docs.text:
On Linux the interpreter creates user, mount and PID namespaces without root, builds a tmpfs root from bind mounts, and calls pivot_root. This is not a chroot: the old root is detached from the process, so there is no path back to it.

Inside, a program sees only its mounts, a private /tmp, a minimal /dev, and its own /proc. A ro mount rejects writes. Other host directories next to a mounted one are invisible. --ro and --deny-exec narrow the sandbox for a single run, and --sandbox chooses what happens when it can't be built, as described below.

docs.title: When the sandbox cannot be created
docs.text:
Some hosts forbid user namespaces: hardened kernels, and containers whose seccomp profile blocks unshare and pivot_root. The --sandbox option, or the WEIR_SANDBOX environment variable, says what to do then. The option wins over the variable.

Mode A sandbox can be built It cannot required (the default) the script runs inside it return code 4, nothing is run auto the script runs inside it a warning naming the cause, then the script runs without it off the script runs without it, with a warning the same

auto is for a machine that is already isolated, such as a CI job in a container. Weir tries to build the sandbox in a short-lived child process before the script starts, so a script never begins inside a half-built one. The --json result says "sandbox": false whenever the script ran without one.

Without a sandbox every path in the script is a host path, so a script with a mount that remaps a path (mount logs at "/logs" ro) can't run that way. That is return code 2 under off, and return code 4 when auto fell back because the sandbox could not be built. --no-sandbox is the same as --sandbox off.

docs.title: A smaller view for one program
docs.text:
A filter's see lines give its program a second, smaller root inside the script's sandbox. Just before the program starts, Weir:

  1. gives the child process its own copy of the mount table (a nested mount namespace);
  2. builds a fresh tmpfs root and bind-mounts only the see paths into it, as ro or rw as written, with a private /tmp, a minimal /dev and /proc;
  3. calls pivot_root into that root and detaches the previous one;
  4. starts the program.
host
 └─ the script's sandbox      user, mount and PID namespaces, pivot_root
     └─ one filter's view     nested mount namespace, pivot_root, only the `see` paths

Paths the script mounted but the filter doesn't see aren't in that program's view at all. The script, and any other filter, still sees them. A see can only narrow: it can't name a path the script didn't mount (E-SEE-UNMOUNTED), and see "/x" ro makes a rw mount read-only for that program.

The nested view changes the filesystem only. The program stays in the same user and PID namespaces as the script.

docs.title: Narrowing part of a flow: within
docs.text:
A within block does for several statements what see lines do for one program. Its header lists the view, and every program started inside it, and the built-ins that touch the filesystem, see only that:

let info = within system, "/etc" ro {
  let kernel = run(cmd: "uname", args: ["-s", "-r"])
  let hosts  = cat_file(file: path(text: "/etc/hosts"))

  return { kernel: first(of: kernel), hosts: count(of: hosts) }
}
  • A value: return leaves the block with a value, so no variable has to be declared outside it. A block used as a value must return on every path (E-WITHIN-NO-RETURN). Variables declared inside the block stay inside it.
  • Only narrower: a within can't widen what the script, or an enclosing within, allows. Naming a path the script never mounted is E-SEE-UNMOUNTED; naming one the enclosing block doesn't have fails when the block starts.
  • Programs: a path outside the view is missing, as it would be for a filter with see lines.
  • Built-ins: read_text, write and the others fail with an error naming the within block. exists returns false.
  • Cost: each program gets its own narrowed root, which adds about 0.6 ms.

The word sandbox is used only for the block at the top of the script. A filter uses see lines, and a flow uses within.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Linux with unprivileged user namespaces only. Tested on Linux 6.12, x86_64.
  • The network is outside the sandbox.
  • The interpreter reaps only the children it starts.

See Implementation status for the full list.
